extracted.intended_audience: covered entities, health care providers and systems, legal counsel, state and local policymakers, and other stakeholders concerned with compliance with section 1557
extracted.subtask_description: Interpreting and applying HHS OCR's final rule implementing section 1557 of the ACA, including scope, relationship to other civil rights statutes, and processes for asserting religious freedom or conscience protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title IX religious exception not imported
rubrics_metrics.description: OCR is finalizing the rule without importing the title IX religious exception into section 1557; OCR proposed and sought comments on not importing the title IX religious exception and responds to commenters in the preamble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR explains that section 1557 'incorporates only the grounds of prohibited discrimination and the enforcement mechanisms' from title IX rather than title IX's exceptions. The preamble gives statutory and practical reasons (text/structure of section 1557, CRRA limitations tied to education, differences between education and health care, and potential harms to access) for declining to import title IX exceptions. OCR also notes that a recipient may still maintain, seek, claim, or assert a title IX religious exception under title IX itself if it meets applicable criteria, and OCR will consider the whole statute in such analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 1557 incorporates only 'grounds prohibited' and enforcement mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1557 incorporates the 'ground[s] prohibited' under referenced civil rights statutes (e.g., sex under title IX) and the enforcement mechanisms provided in those statutes, rather than importing other statutory applicability provisions or exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR emphasizes the ordinary meaning of statutory citations (including 'et seq.') does not expand substantive incorporation; section 1557's wording narrowly references grounds of discrimination and enforcement mechanisms (42 U.S.C. 18116(a)), not the full text or exceptions of the referenced statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: §92.3(a) 'lesser standard' language retained
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed §92.3(a) provided that neither section 1557 nor this part shall be interpreted to apply lesser standards for the protection of individuals from discrimination than the standards under title VI, title IX, section 504, or the Age Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR declines to remove the 'lesser standard' language and reaffirms that nothing in the final rule is intended to provide lesser protections than those statutes or their implementing regulations; this interpretation aligns with a natural reading of 42 U.S.C. 18116(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: §92.3(b) preserves rights, remedies, procedures, and legal standards of referenced statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: §92.3(b) states that nothing in the part shall be interpreted to invalidate or limit the existing rights, remedies, procedures, or legal standards available under the Federal civil rights laws cited in 42 U.S.C. 18116(b) (title VI, title VII, title IX, section 504, and the Age Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR clarifies that section 1557 is an independent civil rights authority that incorporates grounds and enforcement mechanisms but does not limit or alter the interpretation of the referenced statutes. The preamble notes courts have recognized private rights of action under section 1557, and the agency will not use rulemaking to set standards for private litigants (that is for the judiciary).

rubrics_metrics.name: §92.3(c) preserves Federal religious freedom and conscience protections
rubrics_metrics.description: §92.3(c) provides that nothing in this part shall be interpreted to invalidate or limit the existing rights, remedies, procedures, or legal standards available under Federal religious freedom and conscience laws; revised to state that insofar as application of any requirement would violate applicable Federal protections for religious freedom and conscience, such application shall not be required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR lists examples of relevant protections (ACA §18023; Church, Coats-Snowe, Weldon Amendments; RFRA) and explains that recipients may rely on those protections or seek assurance under §92.302. The final rule adds specificity that application of requirements need not be compelled where doing so would violate applicable conscience/religious freedom laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: §92.302 voluntary assurance of exemption process (religious freedom/conscience)
rubrics_metrics.description: OCR adopts a voluntary assurance of exemption process at §92.302 allowing recipients to seek assurance that certain rule requirements will not be applied where federal religious freedom or conscience protections apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR strengthened the process for raising religious freedom and conscience protections, will consider governing statutory standards in making determinations, and commits to trainings and resources to help covered entities understand obligations and the exemption-assurance process.

rubrics_metrics.name: §92.3(d) preserves state/local laws providing additional protections
rubrics_metrics.description: New §92.3(d) provides, 'Nothing in this part shall be construed to supersede State or local laws that provide additional protections against discrimination on any basis described in §92.1.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR added this text to recognize that state or local laws may offer greater protections than section 1557 and that the rule is not intended to preempt laws that provide additional protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal preemption and state law conflicts addressed case-by-case
rubrics_metrics.description: OCR acknowledges that Federal laws generally preempt conflicting State laws and that section 1557 preempts state laws that are contrary to its nondiscrimination protections, but OCR will consider facts and any legitimate nondiscriminatory reasons when evaluating conflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR declines to add broader preemption language to the regulation and explains it will assess specific circumstances in enforcement and complaint contexts rather than adopt categorical preemption rules in the regulation text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscience/religious protections do not compel providers to perform services contrary to beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: A covered entity does not engage in discrimination prohibited by section 1557 if it declines to provide abortions based on religious or conscience objections; nothing in the rule compels providers to perform, cover, or promote procedures to which they have sincerely-held objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR cites ACA 42 U.S.C. 18023(c)(2)(A) and other conscience protections; recipients that believe they are exempt under federal conscience/religious laws may rely on those provisions or seek assurance under §92.302.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between education and health care contexts (limits on importing Title IX exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: OCR explains that many Title IX exceptions are tied to educational settings and have little application to health programs and activities; Title IX's limitation to 'education' supports excluding Title IX exceptions from section 1557's coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR points to examples of Title IX exceptions (fraternities/sororities, youth organizations, beauty pageant-based scholarships, admissions practices) and notes health care contexts (urgency, limited choice, rural access) differ materially, supporting nonimportation of Title IX exceptions into health-care-focused section 1557.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of access and choice considerations in health care
rubrics_metrics.description: OCR repeatedly notes that access to health care, urgency of care, geographic and insurance-related constraints, and fewer choices in selecting providers make the health care context distinct from education and inform the Department's interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR reasons that importing Title IX exceptions could undermine access to health care and that alternative protections (conscience laws, RFRA, ACA provisions) are a better fit to balance religious freedom and access concerns; OCR references its Regulatory Impact Analysis for more detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: IHS and tribal entities treatment (political classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Membership or eligibility in a federally recognized tribal entity is a political classification rather than a racial classification; programs of the Indian Health Service (IHS) are administered by IHS and tribes, including through self-determination contracts or self-governance compacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble notes OCR will apply the Department's title VI regulation exemption for benefits limited by Federal law (45 CFR 80.3(d), e.g., Indian Health and Cuban Refugee Services) and that §92.101(b) adopts such provisions by reference; OCR intends to address any restrictions on application to IHS programs in the context of individual complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: OCR to provide tools and resources for determining covered entity status
rubrics_metrics.description: Some commenters asked OCR to develop an online tool to help covered entities determine whether the final rule applies; OCR states it provides various tools on its website and will continue to assess needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR points stakeholders to the Department Office of Grants TAGGS site (https://taggs.hhs.gov/) to identify recipients of Department funding and indicates it will make trainings and other resources available to assist covered entities in understanding obligations under section 1557.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 1557 is distinct authority and private right of action exists
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1557 provides an independent basis for regulation of discrimination in covered health programs and activities and authorizes private rights of action under the incorporated bases for discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR states it will not adopt regulatory language about administrative exhaustion or litigative standards for private plaintiffs (those issues are for courts). The rule is informed by implementing regulations under other statutes but remains a distinct authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auxiliary aids and services definition retained
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'auxiliary aids and services' was defined in the 2016 Rule and 'has not been changed substantively' in this final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR indicates continuity with the 2016 Rule's definition; no substantive change was made in the definition in §92.4.
